terms.meaning: England's top division. Twenty clubs, each plays the other nineteen twice, August to May.
terms.heard: Constantly. It is the whole thing.

terms.meaning: Three for a win, one for a draw, none for a loss. The table is just points added up.
terms.heard: "Three points is three points" after any ugly win.

terms.meaning: The league standings. Top wins the title, bottom three go down.
terms.heard: "Where are we in the table?" He knows. He wants to say it.

terms.meaning: Goals scored minus goals let in. Splits teams that are level on points.
terms.heard: Late in the season when two teams are neck and neck.

terms.meaning: The bottom three at the end of the season drop down to the Championship.
terms.heard: "Relegation battle" from about February onwards.

terms.meaning: Going up a division. Three come up from the Championship each summer.
terms.heard: In May, usually with someone crying on a pitch.

terms.meaning: The second division, one below the Premier League. Not to be confused with a championship.
terms.heard: "They'll be in the Championship next year" said unkindly.

terms.meaning: In the Championship, the top two go up automatically and the next four fight for the last place.
terms.heard: Late May. The final is called the richest game in football.

terms.meaning: You can't be nearer the goal than the last defender at the moment the ball is played to you.
terms.heard: Every time a flag goes up and someone on the sofa groans.

terms.meaning: Video Assistant Referee. Someone in a room checks goals, penalties and red cards on replay.
terms.heard: "VAR is checking" followed by two minutes of silence.

terms.meaning: VAR is only meant to overturn a decision that was clearly wrong. In practice, opinions differ.
terms.heard: "If it takes that long it isn't clear and obvious."

terms.meaning: Touching the ball with your hand or arm on purpose, or with your arm making you bigger. Goalkeepers are exempt in their box.
terms.heard: "That's handball all day" about a ball that brushed a shoulder.

terms.meaning: A free shot from twelve yards, only the keeper to beat, given for a foul or handball in the box.
terms.heard: A gasp, then nobody speaks until it's taken.

terms.meaning: The big rectangle in front of each goal. Fouls in there are penalties.
terms.heard: "Get it in the box!" whenever a cross is coming.

terms.meaning: A stopped-ball restart after a foul. Direct ones can be shot at goal; indirect ones can't.
terms.heard: "That's a free kick every day of the week."

terms.meaning: When the defending side puts the ball out behind their own goal line, the attackers cross it in from the corner.
terms.heard: "Corners are as good as a goal" said hopefully.

terms.meaning: Ball goes out over the sideline, the other team throws it back in with both hands.
terms.heard: Rarely. Unless someone has a famously long one.

terms.meaning: A warning. Two in one game and you're off.
terms.heard: "He's on a yellow" means the player has to be careful now.

terms.meaning: Sent off. The team plays the rest of the game a player short.
terms.heard: "Straight red" means one bad tackle, no warning first.

terms.meaning: Playing with one fewer after a red card. Teams often sit deep and defend.
terms.heard: "Down to ten men" said either with dread or delight.

terms.meaning: Minutes tacked on at the end of each half for stoppages. Also called injury time or stoppage time.
terms.heard: "How long has he added?" the second the board goes up.

terms.meaning: Two extra fifteen-minute halves in a cup game that's level. Not the same as added time.
terms.heard: In knockout games only. League games just end level.

terms.meaning: If extra time is still level, five penalties each, then one at a time until someone misses.
terms.heard: England fans go quiet at the mention of it.

terms.meaning: In a two-leg cup match, the two scores added together decide who goes through.
terms.heard: European nights. "They're 3-2 up on aggregate."

terms.meaning: Playing the same opponent home and away in a cup round, one game at each ground.
terms.heard: "The second leg is at home" is good news.

terms.meaning: Swapping a player on the pitch for one on the bench. Five allowed per game.
terms.heard: "Bit early for a sub" or "About time."

terms.meaning: The substitutes, sitting beside the pitch waiting to come on.
terms.heard: "He's on the bench" means not starting, but might play.

terms.meaning: The eleven players who begin the match. Announced about an hour before kick-off.
terms.heard: "Team's out" when the line-up appears on his phone.

terms.meaning: Letting in no goals. A goalkeeper's favourite stat.
terms.heard: "Another clean sheet" said with real pride.

terms.meaning: Putting the ball in your own net. Counts for the other team.
terms.heard: A pained "oh no" from the whole room.

terms.meaning: Three goals by one player in one match. They get to keep the ball.
terms.heard: For days afterwards.

terms.meaning: Two goals by the same player in one game.
terms.heard: "He got a brace" in the match report.

terms.meaning: The pass that leads directly to a goal.
terms.heard: "Goals and assists" when he's rating a player.

terms.meaning: The list of upcoming matches. Who plays who, and when.
terms.heard: "Have you seen the fixtures?" in June, when they come out.

terms.meaning: A match between two rivals, usually from the same city or area. Pronounced darby.
terms.heard: The week before, the week of, and the week after.

terms.meaning: Knockout competitions run alongside the league: the FA Cup and the League Cup.
terms.heard: "It's only the cup" when they lose, "a cup run" when they win.

terms.meaning: The oldest cup competition in the world. Every club in England can enter, so tiny teams sometimes play giants.
terms.heard: "The magic of the cup" when a small club wins.

terms.meaning: The smaller cup, named after its sponsor most years. Big clubs often play their reserves.
terms.heard: "Good chance to rest people" from the manager.

terms.meaning: Europe's top club competition. The best clubs from each country, midweek nights, a famous anthem.
terms.heard: Tuesday and Wednesday nights, September to May.

terms.meaning: Europe's second competition, for clubs that finish just below the Champions League places.
terms.heard: "Thursday night football" said with a slight sigh.

terms.meaning: The only times clubs can buy and sell players: the summer, and the month of January.
terms.heard: "Deadline day" on the last day, with a countdown clock.

terms.meaning: The last day of the transfer window. Deals get done at midnight and reporters stand outside stadiums.
terms.heard: Someone shouting "here we go" at a phone.

terms.meaning: Borrowing a player from another club for a season. Common for young players getting experience.
terms.heard: "He's out on loan" about a promising kid.

terms.meaning: How the ten outfield players are arranged, read from the back. 4-3-3 is four defenders, three midfielders, three attackers.
terms.heard: "They've gone 4-4-2" as if it explains everything.

terms.meaning: The four defenders across the pitch in front of the goalkeeper. Two centre-backs and two full-backs.
terms.heard: "The back four were solid" is high praise.

terms.meaning: The two big defenders in the middle. Heading, tackling, organising.
terms.heard: "He's a proper centre-back" means old-fashioned and tough.

terms.meaning: The defenders on either side who also run forward to attack. Busiest job on the pitch.
terms.heard: "The full-backs were up and down all day."

terms.meaning: A full-back who plays higher up the pitch, in a team with three centre-backs behind him.
terms.heard: When a team plays with a back three.

terms.meaning: The midfielder who stays back to protect the defence rather than running forward.
terms.heard: "The six" or "the number six", after the shirt number they used to wear.

terms.meaning: A midfielder who runs from his own penalty area to theirs all game long.
terms.heard: "Proper box-to-box midfielder" said admiringly.

terms.meaning: The creative player who plays just behind the striker and makes the clever passes.
terms.heard: "He's a classic ten" about someone who can't be bothered to defend.

terms.meaning: The player the team's attacks go through. Sees passes others don't.
terms.heard: "He makes them tick" is the phrase.

terms.meaning: An attacker who plays wide near the touchline, dribbles past defenders and crosses.
terms.heard: "Get it wide to the winger!"

terms.meaning: The player whose whole job is scoring. Also called a forward or a number nine.
terms.heard: "They need a striker" about half the clubs in the league.

terms.meaning: A big striker the team aims long balls at. He holds it up and brings others into play.
terms.heard: "Get it up to the big man" when a team is desperate.

terms.meaning: A striker who drops back into midfield instead of staying up front, pulling defenders out of position.
terms.heard: In clever tactical chats. Sounds fancier than it is.

terms.meaning: Chasing the other team the moment they have the ball, high up the pitch, to force mistakes.
terms.heard: "They press really well" about energetic teams.

terms.meaning: Pressing right up near the other team's goal, so they can't even pass out from the back.
terms.heard: When a team wins the ball near the corner flag and scores.

terms.meaning: The whole team sitting deep near their own goal, letting the other side have the ball.
terms.heard: "They've sat in a low block" about a team defending a lead.

terms.meaning: Defending with everyone, no attacking at all. As if a bus were parked across the goal.
terms.heard: Usually as an insult about a boring opponent.

terms.meaning: Winning the ball and racing forward fast before the other team can get back.
terms.heard: "Dangerous on the counter" about quick teams.

terms.meaning: How much of the game a team has the ball. Shown as a percentage on screen.
terms.heard: "Sixty percent possession and nothing to show for it."

terms.meaning: Lots of short, quick passes to keep the ball. Made famous by Barcelona and Spain.
terms.heard: Half in praise, half in mockery.

terms.meaning: Kicking it high and far up the pitch instead of passing it along the ground.
terms.heard: "Route one" is the same idea, said more rudely.

terms.meaning: A defender following one particular attacker everywhere, rather than guarding a space.
terms.heard: "Who's marking him?" after a free header.

terms.meaning: Defenders each guard an area at corners and free kicks, instead of a person.
terms.heard: Blamed for every goal from a corner.

terms.meaning: Any restart from a stopped ball: corners, free kicks, throw-ins. Teams rehearse them.
terms.heard: "Strong from set pieces" about tall teams.

terms.meaning: A full-back running past the winger on the outside to give him a passing option.
terms.heard: "Great overlap" from a co-commentator.

terms.meaning: A pass slid between defenders for a teammate to run onto.
terms.heard: "What a ball" when it works.

terms.meaning: Getting to the byline and passing the ball back across goal for someone to tap in.
terms.heard: Modern teams score half their goals this way.

terms.meaning: A full-back who moves into midfield when his team has the ball, making an extra passer.
terms.heard: Guardiola fans. Sounds very clever.

terms.meaning: The gaps between the middle and the wings where clever attackers like to receive the ball.
terms.heard: Tactics podcasts. Nod if you hear it.

terms.meaning: Expected goals. A number for how good a chance was: a tap-in is nearly 1, a long shot is nearly 0.
terms.heard: "The xG was 2.5 and we lost 1-0" as a complaint.

terms.meaning: Slowing the match down when you're winning: passing it about, taking your time, no risks.
terms.heard: "Good game management" or "cynical", depending on who's winning.

terms.meaning: Hold onto a lead until the final whistle without anything going wrong.
terms.heard: "Just see it out" in the last ten minutes.

terms.meaning: The start of the match, or the start of each half.
terms.heard: "What time's kick-off?" about eight times a weekend.

terms.meaning: The fifteen-minute break in the middle. Kettle time.
terms.heard: "Half-time team talk" when the manager needs to fix things.

terms.meaning: The end of the match. The referee blows and it's over.
terms.heard: "FT" in a text. Then either celebration or silence.

terms.meaning: No goals for either side. Nil is football's word for zero.
terms.heard: "Bore draw" if it was dull, "a tight game" if he's being kind.

terms.meaning: A match between two teams fighting for the same thing, so winning gains three and denies the other three.
terms.heard: Relegation battles in spring, title races in April.

terms.meaning: Finishing in the first four places, which earns a Champions League spot for next season.
terms.heard: "Top four is the aim" from big clubs that won't win the title.

terms.meaning: Two or more teams close at the top of the table with a few games left.
terms.heard: "It's a proper title race" once March arrives.

terms.meaning: Several clubs near the bottom fighting to avoid the last three places.
terms.heard: In spring, with a lot of stress.

terms.meaning: An easy chance that should have been a goal and wasn't.
terms.heard: "How has he missed that?"

terms.meaning: A spectacular goal, usually from far out and hit very hard.
terms.heard: "What a screamer" and then the replay, twice.

terms.meaning: The top corner of the goal. The hardest place to save, the nicest place to score.
terms.heard: "Top bins!" with real joy.

terms.meaning: Poking the ball between a defender's legs and running round him. Humiliating for the defender.
terms.heard: A cheer that has nothing to do with a goal.

terms.meaning: A world-class goal. Short for world-class.
terms.heard: Only for the very best ones.

terms.meaning: A terrible, obvious mistake. Usually by a goalkeeper or a defender.
terms.heard: "Absolute howler" about a ball rolling under someone's foot.

terms.meaning: Launching the ball into the crowded penalty box and hoping. Late-game desperation.
terms.heard: "Just get it in the mixer" in the last minute.

terms.meaning: The simplest way to attack: hoof it long and chase it.
terms.heard: As an insult about direct teams.

terms.meaning: Attacking fast right after winning the ball. Same thing as a counter-attack.
terms.heard: "They caught them on the break."

terms.meaning: Winning a game you were being outplayed in, with one late goal.
terms.heard: Said by whichever side lost.

terms.meaning: A defender losing concentration for a second and letting an attacker get free.
terms.heard: "He's gone to sleep there" after a goal against.

terms.meaning: A match that no longer matters because everything has already been decided.
terms.heard: Last group game of a tournament, or the final league game.

terms.meaning: A small club knocking a big one out of a cup.
terms.heard: FA Cup weekends in January and February.

terms.meaning: A manager screaming at players at half-time, so close their hair moves. Named for Alex Ferguson.
terms.heard: "They'll be getting the hairdryer" after a bad first half.

terms.meaning: The best player on the day, picked by the broadcaster or a sponsor.
terms.heard: "Who's your man of the match?" is a safe question every time.

terms.meaning: Generous added time that seems to appear when a big club needs a goal. Named for Alex Ferguson's Manchester United.
terms.heard: Sarcastically, by fans of every other club.

terms.meaning: The manager. Old British slang for the boss.
terms.heard: "The gaffer's got them playing" from players and pundits alike.

terms.meaning: Also the manager. Players say it so they don't have to say his name.
terms.heard: Post-match interviews. "The boss said to keep going."

terms.meaning: Pundit-speak for very good. Two tops is better than one.
terms.heard: Match of the Day, any week.

terms.meaning: The BBC's Saturday night highlights show. Been going since 1964.
terms.heard: "Just watching MOTD" at 10.30pm on a Saturday.

terms.meaning: An ex-player who talks about the match on TV. Often blamed for having opinions.
terms.heard: "He's a pundit now" about a player who retired.

terms.meaning: The team. How players and fans refer to their own side.
terms.heard: "Proud of the lads" after a hard game.

terms.meaning: To lose your nerve at the crucial moment and throw away something you should have won.
terms.heard: Cruelly, about title races that collapsed.

terms.meaning: Teasing between fans. Mostly friendly, occasionally not.
terms.heard: "It's just banter" after a text that went slightly too far.

terms.meaning: Where his mates react to every goal in real time. Louder than the stadium.
terms.heard: His phone buzzing eleven times in a row after a goal.

terms.meaning: A pass for every home league game. Waiting lists at big clubs can be years long.
terms.heard: "I've had a season ticket since I was eight."

terms.meaning: Travelling to watch the team play at another ground. Trains, pubs, singing.
terms.heard: "Big away day" when it's somewhere far or somewhere fun.

terms.meaning: The section of the stadium where travelling fans sit. Usually the loudest.
terms.heard: "Listen to the away end" when the home fans have gone quiet.

terms.meaning: Liverpool's famous home stand, where the loudest fans sing. Other grounds borrowed the name.
terms.heard: Anfield nights on TV.

terms.meaning: The old standing areas at football grounds. Now mostly seats, but the word stuck for the fans.
terms.heard: "Terrace chant" about a song the crowd sings.

terms.meaning: A song sung by the crowd, usually to a pop tune with new words about a player.
terms.heard: Him humming one in the kitchen.

terms.meaning: A souvenir scarf with both teams' colours. Proper fans find them embarrassing.
terms.heard: Mocked outside every big game.

terms.meaning: Someone accused of supporting a team only because it's successful.
terms.heard: Thrown at fans of whoever is winning.

terms.meaning: A fan who picked a team for its trophies rather than any real connection.
terms.heard: "Typical glory hunter" about a mate who supports a club far away.

terms.meaning: Liverpool's old coaching room where managers were quietly promoted from within. Now means a club that grows its own.
terms.heard: History chats about how Liverpool used to run things.

terms.meaning: Arsenal's 2003-04 team, who went the whole league season without losing.
terms.heard: From every Arsenal fan, about twice a year.

terms.meaning: The unofficial contest for which manager gets fired first each season.
terms.heard: "He's favourite in the sack race" after three losses.

terms.meaning: The short burst of good results a team often gets right after changing manager.
terms.heard: "Just the bounce" when a new manager wins his first two.

terms.meaning: The summer, when there's no football and every transfer rumour gets printed.
terms.heard: "Ignore it, it's silly season" about a wild headline.

terms.meaning: Transfer reporter Fabrizio Romano's phrase for a deal that is definitely happening.
terms.heard: Screenshot in the group chat with several exclamation marks.

terms.meaning: The online corner where fans argue about everything, all day, forever.
terms.heard: "Football Twitter is going mad" about anything at all.

terms.meaning: An online game where you pick real players and score points from their real performances.
terms.heard: "He's in my fantasy team" about a player he's suddenly cheering for.

terms.meaning: Old tabloid slang for players' wives and girlfriends. Mostly retired now, thankfully.
terms.heard: In stories about the 2006 World Cup.

terms.meaning: The old joke about physios fixing any injury with a wet sponge. Players got up instantly.
terms.heard: Ironically, when a player recovers very quickly.

terms.meaning: Match of the Day's pick of the best goal, voted by viewers.
terms.heard: "That's goal of the month" about any long-range strike.

terms.meaning: The idea that anything can happen in the FA Cup. A small team beating a big one proves it.
terms.heard: Commentators, the moment a non-league side scores.
